summary: FairTutor is a work-in-progress tutoring cascade. A cheap model (Qwen3-8B) drafts an answer, a cheap evaluator scores it on a seven-part pedagogy rubric, a critic rewrites borderline answers, and only failures go to GPT-5. On 50 synthetic single-turn student queries judged by GPT-5, it reports 97.1% of premium quality at 28.4% of premium token cost. Its margin over a plain generic cascade is not statistically resolved.

claims.claim: FairTutor achieves 97.1% of premium pedagogical quality while reducing serving cost by 71.6%
claims.evidence: Tables 1-2: quality 4.760 vs 4.874 (premium), cost 28.4% of premium. Cost is a token-weighted proxy with assumed 100x/75x price ratios and excludes evaluator calls. Quality is judged by GPT-5, which is also the premium tutor. n=50, single sample per system.

claims.claim: FairTutor beats the generic cascade router
claims.evidence: Appendix B: paired bootstrap gain over generic cascade +0.065, 95% CI [-0.040, +0.168], which spans zero. The author concedes this is not resolved at n=50.

claims.claim: FairTutor substantially closes the access-tier gap relative to the low-cost-only baseline
claims.evidence: Appendix B: per-query gain over low-cost-only +0.360, 95% CI [+0.203, +0.533]; ranking preserved under an independent DeepSeek-V4 judge (r=0.53 with GPT-5). Any cascade that escalates 18% of queries to the premium model would be expected to beat low-cost-only.

claims.claim: Sweeping the escalation threshold τ traces a smooth cost-quality Pareto frontier
claims.evidence: Appendix C, Table 5: offline replay over fixed, single-sample generations; τ=4.5 gives 100% within-0.5 parity at 33.9% cost; escalation climbs steeply beyond τ≈4.6. Same 50 queries and same judge.

patterns.note: Cheap-first cascade with an evaluator threshold and a rewrite band before escalation. Evidence is 50 synthetic queries and an LLM judge; no margin over a generic cascade.
A cheap LLM evaluator gates escalation; final scoring by GPT-5 (also the premium tutor) agrees with DeepSeek-V4 only at r=0.53.
Six-role pipeline (analyzer, planner, tutor, evaluator, critic, escalation controller); roles are not ablated individually.

methodology.sample: 50 synthetic single-turn K-12 tutoring queries (TutorAccessEval WIP); 250 responses
methodology.baselines: Low-cost-only, premium-only, naive difficulty router, generic cascade — all author-built; no RouteLLM/FrugalGPT
methodology.models: Qwen3-8B (cheap), GPT-5 (premium and evaluator); DeepSeek-V4 re-judge
methodology.variance: SE of mean; paired bootstrap CIs; single generation sample per stage
methodology.ablations: Threshold sweep via offline replay; no per-component ablation (planner, critic)
methodology.languages: English (plus one French translation item); no code

standards.peer_review: Workshop (AI for Education Day at SIGKDD 2026), self-described WIP
standards.artifacts: Code under MIT at github.com/qyxu1994/fairtutor-router; dataset described in Appendix D

biases.detail: 50 queries; the headline comparison against the strongest baseline has a CI spanning zero.
GPT-5 judges its own premium answers; the second judge correlates at r=0.53; no educator annotation.
All baselines are author-built; published routers are deferred to future work.
Cost excludes evaluator calls and is a token proxy with assumed price ratios.
Synthetic single-turn queries; no student learning outcome measured.
Author designs the rubric, benchmark, system, and baselines.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Qwen3-8B, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V4 used as components, not promoted
coi.detail: No vendor affiliation; the paper is not a product announcement.

verdict_reason: Honest WIP with code release and its own bootstrap showing the key comparison is unresolved. Only the trivial claim (a cascade beats cheap-only) is supported; the 97.1%/71.6% headline rests on one GPT-5-judged run over 50 synthetic queries.
applicability: Not a coding-agent paper. For a healthcare-education content team it is at most a sketch for a learner-facing product: a cheap-first answer path with a rubric gate and escalation. It gives no evidence for any coding-harness decision.
